title: Berkshire 2018 letter: five groves, float, buybacks, and the American Tailwind
summary: Buffett explains how to value Berkshire as a forest of five asset groves rather than trees, why GAAP mark-to-market and book value mislead, how float and retained earnings fund growth, and why disciplined buybacks, minimal debt and a cash fortress matter. He closes with faith in American business.

principles.text: Ignore GAAP gains and losses on holdings; focus on operating earnings.
principles.quote: Our advice? Focus on operating earnings, paying little attention to gains or losses of any variety.

principles.text: Buy ably-managed businesses with durable economics at sensible prices, whole or in part.
principles.quote: our prime goal in the deployment of your capital: to buy ably-managed businesses, in whole or part, that possess favorable and durable economic characteristics. We also need to make these purchases at sensible prices.

principles.text: Repurchases only make sense below intrinsic value; blind buying of an overpriced stock destroys value.
principles.quote: Obviously, repurchases should be price-sensitive: Blindly buying an overpriced stock is value-destructive, a fact lost on many promotional or ever-optimistic CEOs.

principles.text: Don't risk what you have and need for what you don't have and don't need; use debt sparingly and keep a cash buffer.
principles.quote: Rational people don't risk what they have and need for what they don't have and don't need.

principles.text: Float is valuable only with disciplined underwriting; poor underwriting can drown its benefits.
principles.quote: Disciplined risk evaluation is the daily focus of our insurance managers, who know that the benefits of float can be drowned by poor underwriting results.

principles.text: Never play with numbers to meet Wall Street expectations; small fudges can lead to fraud.
principles.quote: Playing with the numbers "just this once" may well be the CEO's intent; it's seldom the end result.
